1.pericope_label: I beseech you, walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called

schools.summary: Read the verse as a rule for teachers — that whoever seeks esteem rather than his hearers’ salvation is a tyrant and not a teacher — and take Paul’s manner of entreaty as the model.
Prefer prisoner for the Lord’s sake, treat the imprisonment as the seal of his commission rather than a discredit, and set out the structure of the remaining chapters before expounding.
Read the bonds as recommending the letter, since a doctrine worth suffering for is worth regarding, and notice that the prisoner asks nothing for himself.

Derive the particular graces required from the particular argument of the letter — aliens now made one body — rather than from a general catalogue of virtues; and explain the grammar and the Colossians parallel.
Take the imprisonment as a motive to obedience that would comfort him, and preface the chapter with its argument.

debates: Whether in the Lord qualifies prisoner or beseech — Gill reports both constructions and prefers the first.

Why Paul names his chains: as a refusal to be ashamed of them (Henry), as confirmation of his apostolic authority (Calvin), as a motive of comfort to be answered by obedience (Wesley), or as a reproach to those whose walk added to his afflictions (Gill).
Whether the graces required by the calling are a general list of Christian virtues or specifically humility and gentleness, drawn from what this letter has said the calling was (Ellicott).
outliers: Chrysostom alone makes the verse a definition of the teaching office, and alone stages Paul’s motive as a dialogue.
Calvin alone ranks the apostle’s prison above the triumphal chariot of kings.
Henry alone dwells on what the prisoner refrains from asking.

2.pericope_label: Lowliness, meekness, long-suffering; keeping the unity of the Spirit

schools.summary: Read the four graces as a strict sequence in which humility is first and forbearance last, trace all breaches of unity to excessive self-love, and prefer harmony of views to the reading that makes the Spirit the producer of the unity — while allowing that the union is of souls and wrought by the Spirit.
Define each grace against the vice it opposes, and gather the whole under love as the law, lesson and livery of Christ’s household.

Deny that of the Spirit refers to the one Holy Spirit and make it unity of affection; explain the danger of division from the Jewish and Gentile composition of the church; and trace the danger of division to the permanent variety of human temperament.

Give the lexical alternatives for forbearing — sustaining one another, or bearing with one another — press the verb for endeavouring as intense labour, and treat the unity as both spiritual in kind and from the Spirit in origin.

debates: Whether the unity of the Spirit means unity produced by the Holy Spirit or unity of a spiritual kind — Calvin reports the first and prefers the second, Barnes denies the first outright, Gill and Clarke take both.
Whether the participle means sustaining one another under life’s burdens or bearing with one another’s faults — Clarke gives both without choosing.
Whether the bond is peace or love — Robertson notes the parallel epistle makes love the bond, and Wesley identifies the two.
outliers: Calvin alone argues that the graces must be cultivated in the order given, and that exhorting to forbearance before humility is wasted labour.
Gill alone infers from the command to keep the unity that it already exists, is valuable, and is hard to hold.
Barnes alone generalises the danger of division from the Ephesian situation to every society of men.

4.pericope_label: One body, one Spirit, one hope; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God

schools.summary: Read the seven unities as an embryo creed rather than a catalogue; refuse to call the Spirit it; deny any intermediate beings beside the one Lord; guard the one baptism against being made the instrument of discipleship; and use the passage to locate the true fault-line of Christian division in the article on the Church rather than in the doctrine of God.
Extend the one body through all time to include those who pleased God before Christ came, and note that Paul grounds his weightiest exhortations on heavenly examples.

Require union of the whole man, and argue from the single inheritance that eternal life cannot be had without harmony here; multiply the figures of the body — natural, political and domestic — and guard the divine unity against any denial of the trinity of persons.
Resolve the seven into the Trinity and the hope of heaven, and read the one baptism as administered in the threefold name and indicative of the whole Christian dispensation.

debates: What the one body includes: the faithful of every age, with the saints before Christ (Chrysostom), or the church of Jews and Gentiles now divided into denominations that ought to feel their oneness (Barnes).
Whether the one baptism is the act or its result, and whether it makes disciples or only professes them — Robertson insists on the second in each case.
Where the real divisions of Christendom lie — Ellicott argues they turn on the doctrine of the Church and not on the doctrine of God.
outliers: Barnes alone names the denominations of his own country, and alone denies that Christ died for men of one colour rather than another.
Robertson alone objects to the neuter pronoun for the Spirit on grammatical grounds while refusing its theological consequence.
Ellicott alone treats the passage as a fragment of a primitive creed.

7.pericope_label: Grace according to the measure of the gift; he ascended, he descended

schools.summary: Read the grace as office, matched to the station each fills; argue that the ascent implies a descent only if the one ascending is God; supply the Roman triumph behind the imagery; and leave the lower parts undecided between the womb and the grave while confining the filling to the church.

State the difficulty of the quotation without disguise, explain the change from received to gave from a known use of the verb and from the Targum’s own gloss, and prefer the descent into the regions beneath the earth on the usage of the phrase and the consent of the ancients.

Concede that Paul departs from the quotation’s plain sense and defend him by denying that he is reasoning as a logician; hold the Psalm’s ascent to be God’s and not David’s; make the measure of grace an argument for mutual dependence and against pride; and deny that Christ’s heaven is any place among the spheres.
Note that the measure of grace is never perfected in this life, since God’s children go on growing while they are in the world.
Take the ascension as the article of the Creed that follows the resurrection.

debates: What the grace given to each is: a particular office (Clarke), the Spirit’s gracious influences (Barnes), the one grace of Christ apportioned by capacity (Ellicott), or either saving grace or ministerial gift (Gill).
On what principle Paul applies a psalm about the ark to the ascension — Barnes says the difficulty is real, Calvin concedes the departure from the plain sense and shifts the ground of the defence.
Why Paul writes gave where the Psalm has received — Ellicott answers from the verb’s use for fetching on another’s behalf and from the Targum’s identical gloss.

Whether the lower parts of the earth means the earth as lower than heaven, and so the incarnation (Barnes, Clarke, Robertson), or the regions beneath it, and so the descent to the dead (Ellicott, with the ancient interpreters).
Whether fill all things is unlimited (Ellicott) or means the church filled with his Spirit (Wesley).
outliers: Calvin alone states the charge of unfair quotation in his opponents’ own words before answering it.
Wesley alone makes the inference from ascent to descent depend on the deity of the one who ascends.
Clarke alone renders the whole verse as a Roman triumph, clause by clause.

11.pericope_label: He gave some apostles; for the perfecting of the saints; till we all come

schools.summary: Read the ministers as themselves gifts because the verb is gave; admit that the office of evangelist can no longer be defined; dispute the threefold parallelism of the English against the Greek prepositions; and set the oneness of faith and knowledge against Gnostic teaching.

Explain why offices are named where gifts are in question, since God never gives the title without the endowment; defend the necessity of a human ministry against the objection that God could order his church without it; treat the apostolate as an extraordinary office now ceased; and prefer to render the disputed noun by a word for civil ordering.

Complain that the distinct gifts survive but are all compounded into the single class of preacher; build on the threefold symmetry of the verses; and press the full measure of the stature as a standard the church declines to be measured by.

debates: Whether the three clauses of verse 12 stand in parallel — Ellicott argues from the change of preposition that they do not, while Wesley builds an elaborate symmetry on the assumption that they do.
What perfecting means: mending or repair (Robertson), restoration to place and completion (Barnes), or the orderly arrangement of a commonwealth (Calvin, against the older rendering).
Whether the perfect man implies sinless perfection — denied by Barnes, who means only maturity, and pressed hard by Clarke as a standard of holiness the church evades.
Whether the unity of the faith is unity of doctrine or the common grace of faith — Gill offers both after excluding two other senses.
outliers: Ellicott alone makes the ministers themselves the gifts, on the strength of the verb.
Clarke alone charges the churches of his own day with collapsing five distinct offices into the single trade of preaching.
Calvin alone states, and answers, the objection that God could have ordered his church without human ministers.

14.pericope_label: No more children, tossed to and fro; speaking the truth in love; the body fitly joined

schools.summary: Limit the childishness meant to impulsiveness and instability rather than to any quality Christ commended; render the participle being true and make constancy in the truth the true antithesis to instability; and correct the English of the body metaphor against the Greek.
Keep a good sense of childhood alongside the bad, and insert a middle stage between infancy and manhood, so that the believer’s life is always youth and never full maturity in this world.

Distinguish the instability that comes from within from the assault that comes from without; take the sleight from the false dice of gamesters; admit ignorance of the other figure; and make the verse a rule against abusive controversy.

debates: In what sense Christians should cease to be children — Ellicott confines the word to a bad sense throughout, while Gill lists respects in which they should remain children still.
Whether the participle means speaking the truth (Barnes) or being true and holding fast to it (Ellicott, and Calvin’s editor) — the second makes constancy, not candour, the point.
What the two participles describe: one danger or two, inward fluctuation and outward assault (Wesley).
outliers: Calvin alone denies that believers reach manhood at all in this life, making the whole Christian course an adolescence.
Clarke alone calls scolding and abuse in religious controversy monstrous, and denies that truth needs any defence but love.
Robertson alone appeals to modern cell biology in support of the apostle’s metaphor.

17.pericope_label: Walk not as other Gentiles; the understanding darkened; past feeling

schools.summary: Analyse the escalating solemnity of the introduction; deny that the darkening was judicial and explain it as the ordinary effect of vice on the mind; construe the life of God as the life God gives; and analyse the escalating solemnity with which the exhortation is introduced.
Justify the severity as a teacher’s duty to alarm as well as instruct, and admire the tact by which Paul draws his example from others rather than charging his readers directly.

Trace the darkening to the fall and the ambition to be as God; distinguish three kinds of life, animal, human and supernatural; and describe the hardening as the accumulation of offences under a conscience that still accuses.

Make the darkness cumulative rather than original, connect it with idolatry, report the variant reading despairing, and explain the force of past feeling from the office of pain in driving the sick to a remedy.
Take the passage as the turn from unity and love to purity and holiness, urged on the conscience by apostolic authority.

debates: Whether the darkening of the understanding is a judicial act of God (denied explicitly by Barnes), the standing consequence of the fall (Gill), or the cumulative effect of habitual sin (Clarke).
Whether the text reads past feeling or despairing — the second is in the Latin, Syriac and Arabic versions and an old Greek copy, and is reported by Gill and Clarke.
How they gave themselves over stands with the statement elsewhere that God gave them up — Barnes denies any inconsistency, Wesley stresses that it was of their own accord.
What the life of God means: life in God’s estimation, or the life he bestows in regeneration — Calvin gives both and treats them as one.
outliers: Chrysostom alone points out the accusation Paul deliberately did not make.
Calvin alone divides life into three kinds and assigns the third to believers only.
Clarke alone suggests that men without hope of blessedness would have an interest in denying the resurrection.

20.pericope_label: Ye have not so learned Christ; put off the old man, put on the new

schools.summary: Take the Christ as a title of office distinct from the personal name (Ellicott) or, against the Gnostics, as identified with it (Robertson); deny that the conditional carries real doubt, though Barnes allows a delicate one; correct taught by him to taught in him; and read corrupt as decay rather than pollution.

Make the passage a test of professed knowledge, since a life like an unbeliever’s proves nothing has been learned; distinguish a genuine from a counterfeit knowledge of Christ; and define the putting off of the old man precisely as a deposing rather than a destroying.
Report the alternative pointing of the clause, and allow no qualification to the renunciation, the whole former life having been corrupt.
Turn the passage into an appeal to the unbaptised, to prepare through faith for the new birth into freedom and adoption.

debates: Whether the Christ is here distinguished from Jesus as a title of office (Ellicott) or deliberately identified with him against the Gnostic separation of the two (Robertson).
Whether if so be that implies real doubt — denied by Ellicott, Robertson and Clarke, allowed as slight and delicate by Barnes.
Whether the clause should be repointed as two propositions, ye are not so; ye have learned Christ — reported by both Gill and Clarke.
How far the renunciation extends: to everything of the former life (Clarke) or only to what belonged to the corrupt nature, dress and manners not being in question (Barnes).
outliers: Gill alone insists that the old man is neither removed, destroyed nor altered, but only deposed from government.
Barnes alone infers from the wording that Ephesus had teachers who neglected practical duties.
Ellicott alone reads corrupt as disintegration, matching the epithet old.

25.pericope_label: Putting away lying; be ye angry and sin not; give no place to the devil

schools.summary: Ask what falsehood is meant and answer that it is not idolatry but the deceit that passes between neighbours.
Define a lie exactly enough to exempt fiction and honest error while refusing the officious lie; and derive every particular exhortation from the righteousness of the new man as from a fountain.

Explain the need of the command by the character of heathen society; distinguish the reason Paul gives from other true reasons that are not to his purpose here; call the imperative permissive; and defend righteous anger from Christ’s own example while marking its danger.
Produce ancient authorities for the low value set on truth among the heathen; and deny that anger without sin is practically attainable, turning the imperative into a warning against anger itself.
Define what it is to give place to the devil — not grieving at the first motions of sin, consenting to them, and repeating the deed.

debates: Whether be ye angry commands, permits, or effectively forbids: a permissive imperative (Robertson), a recognition that anger may be sinless though perilous (Barnes, Gill), a defence of righteous indignation as a weapon against evil (Ellicott), or a warning that even an apostle could hardly be angry without sin (Clarke).
What kind of falsehood is forbidden — idolatry is raised and set aside by Chrysostom in favour of ordinary deceit between neighbours.
Whether an officious lie told for another’s benefit is lawful — Gill raises the case and denies it.
Why the reason given is membership one of another rather than duty to God or to truth itself — Ellicott insists the other reasons, though true, are beside the apostle’s argument.
outliers: Barnes alone supports his account of heathen mendacity from the testimony of a colonial jurist and of missionaries; Clarke makes a similar claim but quotes ancient authors for it.
Clarke alone denies that the verse can be a precept at all.
Ellicott alone enlists a modern moral philosopher in defence of resentment.

28.pericope_label: Let him that stole steal no more; no corrupt communication; grieve not the Holy Spirit

schools.summary: Define theft to include concealed frauds and withheld wages; face the objection that the command would bind every man to manual labour and answer that it is aimed at the plea of want; and prefer the reading that makes the genitive the progress of edification.

Explain the caution by the prevalence of theft among the heathen and the power of habit; read the positive clause as a supersession of dishonesty by self-sacrifice; give the lexical sense of the word for corrupt; correct the English rendering of the clause about edifying; and argue that grieving implies a personal relation to the Spirit stronger than quenching or resisting.

Reject the alleged rabbinic allowance of theft where alms follow; classify the senses of the word for corrupt from the lexicographers; and trace what follows on the Spirit’s withdrawal — darkness, hardness, and insensibility.
Trace filthy speech to corruption in the speaker and its effect on the hearer, and connect it to the grieving of the Spirit who is the earnest of the redemption day.
Turn from the warning to the Spirit’s operation, instancing the wisdom given to Daniel by which a condemned woman was delivered.

debates: Whether the command to labour with the hands binds all Christians to manual work: Calvin raises the objection, calls the literal sense excessively hard, and limits the clause to the excuse of want.
Whether stealing may be excused by charity with the proceeds — reported as a rabbinic allowance by Clarke and refused.

How to render the clause about edifying: the received English (assumed by Barnes, Clarke and Wesley) against Ellicott’s “building up of the need”, with Calvin weighing the same genitive and deciding differently.
Whether the Spirit is grieved in himself or grieved in godly brethren whom we offend — Calvin reports the second view and rejects it.
In what sense grief can be predicated of God: an anthropopathy (Gill), a description of conduct fitted to cause grief (Barnes), or evidence of a real personal relation (Ellicott).
outliers: Barnes alone infers from the verse that dependence on others is unlawful for any man able to work.
Clarke alone follows the withdrawal of the Spirit through to insensibility, in which the loss itself can no longer be perceived.
Cyril alone treats the verse as an occasion for the Spirit’s works rather than for warning.

31.pericope_label: Put away bitterness, wrath, anger, clamour and evil speaking; be kind, tenderhearted, forgiving

schools.summary: Read the catalogue as an ascending progression from acerbity of temper through passionate outburst to deliberate slander, all exhibitions of malice; gloss the individual terms and correct the rendering of the last; and treat the answering virtues as disposition, with forgiveness that neither condones evil nor withholds chastisement.

Read the same catalogue as a descent from the highest degree of the want of love to the lowest, pairing each term with its opposing virtue; identify bitterness with religious censoriousness; and distinguish the two words for anger as the beginning and the extremity of one passion.
Range the senses of bitterness and settle on the first inward offence taken; deny that the two words for anger differ here as power and act; and note that removing malice would correct the rest.

Argue the case by images — the hive no bees will enter, the bile that poisons the body once its vessel breaks — and ground the command to forgive on what God has already done rather than on the promise of future pardon.

debates: Whether the list ascends or descends: Ellicott’s three rising stages from bitterness to evil speaking against Wesley’s retrogradation from the height of settled anger down to the first risings of disgust.
What bitterness denotes — the corruption of nature, false doctrine, or simply the first offence taken in the mind (Gill), against Clarke’s identification of it with religious censoriousness.
Whether the two words for anger differ as power and act: the received distinction, reported and set aside by Calvin, against Clarke’s beginning-and-extremity reading.
Whether the answering virtue is courtesy of manner (Barnes, Clarke) or an inward disposition only (Ellicott, Calvin).
Whether the participle in the last clause means to forgive or to be beneficent — Calvin reports the second rendering and prefers the first.
outliers: Clarke alone names an apothecary’s preparation to supply an epithet for the censorious.
Chrysostom alone argues from apiculture and from physiology rather than from the text’s wording.
Barnes alone treats politeness as a Christian duty and denies religion to a sour temper.
Ellicott alone qualifies the command to forgive by excluding condonation and the remission of chastisement.
